criteria.explanation: Checks for a linter config (ruff, eslint, etc.). A linter catches bugs and anti-patterns mechanically, so an agent gets consistent, automated feedback instead of guessing the project's standards.
criteria.remediation: Add a linter config for your stack — a `[tool.ruff]` block in `pyproject.toml` for Python, or `biome.json` / `eslint.config.mjs` for JS/TS — and commit it. Praxion's `/onboard-project` scaffolds this automatically (Phase 8e).

criteria.explanation: Checks for an auto-formatter config (ruff format, black, prettier). A formatter removes style debate and keeps diffs minimal, so agent edits stay consistent with the codebase automatically.
criteria.remediation: Configure a formatter — `[tool.ruff.format]` / black for Python or Biome / Prettier for JS/TS — and pin its settings in the project config. Praxion's `/onboard-project` scaffolds this (Phase 8e).

criteria.explanation: Checks for an `.editorconfig`. It encodes indentation, charset, and newline rules every editor honors, so contributors and agents emit byte-consistent files regardless of local settings.
criteria.remediation: Add an `.editorconfig` at the repo root declaring `indent_style`, `indent_size`, `end_of_line`, and `charset` for your file types. Praxion's `/onboard-project` installs a universal one (Phase 8e).

criteria.explanation: Checks for a pre-commit hook config. Running lint/format/secret checks before each commit shifts quality enforcement left, so bad changes are blocked at authoring time rather than in review.
criteria.remediation: Add a `.pre-commit-config.yaml` wiring your linter, formatter, and secret scanner, then run `pre-commit install`.

criteria.explanation: An LLM judges whether names are consistent and intention-revealing across the codebase. Predictable naming lets an agent locate and extend code without re-reading everything.
criteria.rationale: The artifact continues to exhibit inconsistent naming conventions across the project structure, with a mix of kebab-case (`.ai-state`, `.ai-work`, `.claude-plugin`), snake_case (`.pytest_cache`, `.ruff_cache`, `new_project.sh`), and UPPERCASE entries (LICENSE, Makefile, README.md), creating maintainability challenges.
criteria.remediation: Establish and document a naming convention policy in a CONTRIBUTING.md or STYLE_GUIDE.md file that specifies: use snake_case for all shell scripts and Python files, kebab-case for dotdir names if needed but standardize to snake_case, and UPPERCASE only for LICENSE and essential top-level configs. Then systematically rename scripts like `new_project.sh` → `new_project.py` and dotdirs like `.ai-work` → `.ai_work` to align with the chosen standard.

criteria.explanation: Checks for a dependency/build manifest (`pyproject.toml`, `package.json`, `Cargo.toml`, …). It declares how to install and build the project — the entry point any agent needs to act safely.
criteria.remediation: Add the manifest for your ecosystem and declare dependencies and build/run entry points in it.

criteria.explanation: Checks for a lockfile (`uv.lock`, `package-lock.json`, …). Pinned transitive versions make installs reproducible, so an agent's local build matches CI and teammates.
criteria.remediation: Generate and commit a lockfile — e.g. `uv lock`, `npm install`, or `poetry lock` — alongside the manifest.

criteria.explanation: Checks for a CI config (GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, …). Automated build/test on every push gives an agent a trusted signal that a change is safe before it merges.
criteria.rationale: a CI pipeline configuration is present
criteria.remediation: Add a CI workflow (e.g. `.github/workflows/test.yml`) that installs dependencies and runs the build and test suite on push/PR.

criteria.explanation: Checks for tests on disk (a `tests/` dir or `*_test`/`test_*` files). Tests are the safety net that lets an agent change code and verify it still works.
criteria.rationale: a test directory or test files are present
criteria.remediation: Create a `tests/` directory and add at least one test that exercises a core behavior, runnable with your test runner.

criteria.explanation: Checks that CI actually invokes the test suite. Tests that don't run automatically rot; wiring them into CI keeps the safety net live on every change.
criteria.rationale: CI configuration invokes the test suite
criteria.remediation: Add a test-run step to your CI workflow (e.g. `pytest -q` or `npm test`) so every push and PR executes the suite.

criteria.explanation: An LLM judges whether tests verify behavior (not implementation details) and meaningfully cover the code. High-quality tests give an agent confidence that green means correct.
criteria.rationale: The artifact is only a file listing that shows testing infrastructure exists (tests directory, .pytest_cache, coverage.xml) but provides no visibility into actual test quality metrics, test coverage percentages, test organization, or test execution results needed to assess whether testing standards are met.
criteria.remediation: Provide the actual contents of the tests directory, coverage.xml metrics (or coverage report output), and pyproject.toml configuration to reveal test organization, coverage thresholds, and quality standards being enforced.

criteria.explanation: Checks for a README. It is the first artifact a human or agent reads to orient — what the project is, how to run it, where things live.
criteria.remediation: Add a `README.md` covering what the project does, how to install and run it, and how to run the tests.

criteria.explanation: Checks for a contributing guide. It encodes the dev workflow — branching, commits, review, release — so a contributor or agent follows the project's process instead of inventing one.
criteria.remediation: Add a `CONTRIBUTING.md` describing the branch/commit conventions, how to run checks locally, and the PR/review flow.

criteria.explanation: An LLM judges whether the README clearly explains setup, usage, and architecture. A present-but-thin README still leaves an agent guessing; this measures whether it actually informs.
criteria.rationale: The README is comprehensive, well-structured, and effectively communicates Praxion's purpose, architecture, and value proposition. It includes clear navigation via a Contents section, status badges, quantified features (49 skills, 15 agents, 39 commands, 20 rules), platform-specific quick-start commands with installation instructions, extensive cross-linked documentation covering core concepts and workflows, detailed feature tables with activation triggers, clear articulation of guiding principles and the behavioral contract, and appropriate depth that serves both new users and contributors.
criteria.remediation: Expand the README with concrete setup steps, a usage example, and a short architecture overview pointing to key directories.

criteria.explanation: An LLM judges whether docs are structured for agent consumption — explicit commands, file-path references, and conventions an agent can act on directly rather than prose it must interpret.
criteria.rationale: The artifact maintains exceptional agent-friendliness through comprehensive hierarchical structure with clear indexing (skills, agents, commands, rules), consistent semantic markup (badges, collapsible details, code blocks, internal cross-references), extensive structured tables with activation triggers and descriptions, and robust navigation aids (detailed table of contents, linked documentation, role-organized sections) that enable agents to efficiently parse and traverse information across multiple abstraction levels.
criteria.remediation: Add agent-facing structure: a CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md with exact build and test commands, repo-layout table, and pointers to conventions.

criteria.explanation: Checks for a `.gitignore`. It keeps build output, caches, and secrets out of version control, so an agent's commits stay clean and don't leak local artifacts.
criteria.remediation: Add a `.gitignore` (start from a GitHub template for your stack) covering build output, caches, virtualenvs, and `.env` files.

criteria.explanation: Checks for a container/devcontainer config (`Dockerfile`, `devcontainer.json`, `compose.yaml`). A reproducible environment removes 'works on my machine' for humans and agents alike.
criteria.remediation: Add a `Dockerfile` or `.devcontainer/devcontainer.json` that provisions the toolchain and dependencies the project needs.

criteria.explanation: Checks for an env-var example (`.env.example`). It documents which configuration the project expects without committing secrets, so setup is self-describing.
criteria.remediation: Add a `.env.example` listing every required variable with safe placeholder values, and reference it from the README.

criteria.explanation: Checks for logging/observability configuration. Structured logging gives an agent runtime evidence to diagnose failures instead of reasoning blind.
criteria.remediation: Add a logging configuration (level, format, handlers) or an observability setup (OpenTelemetry, structured logger) to the app.

criteria.explanation: Checks for a health-check or monitoring surface (a `/health` endpoint, a healthcheck script). It lets automation confirm the service is actually up, not just deployed.
criteria.remediation: Expose a health endpoint or check (e.g. `/healthz`) and wire it into your container/deploy config or monitoring.

criteria.explanation: Checks for automated dependency vulnerability scanning (Dependabot, renovate, audit in CI). It surfaces known CVEs in dependencies before they ship.
criteria.remediation: Enable `.github/dependabot.yml` or add an audit step (`pip-audit`, `npm audit`) to CI.

criteria.explanation: Checks for secrets hygiene (a secret scanner config, or a documented secrets policy). It guards against committing credentials — a failure mode agents are especially prone to.
criteria.remediation: Add a secret scanner (gitleaks/trufflehog) to pre-commit or CI, and document where real secrets belong.

criteria.explanation: Checks for a LICENSE file. It defines how the code may be used and is a baseline governance signal for any shared project.
criteria.remediation: Add a `LICENSE` file with an SPDX-recognized license appropriate to the project.

criteria.explanation: Checks for a static type-checker config (mypy, pyright, tsconfig strict). Types catch a class of errors before runtime and document interfaces an agent must respect.
criteria.remediation: Configure a type checker — a `[tool.mypy]`/`pyrightconfig.json` for Python or `strict` in `tsconfig.json` for TS — and run it in CI.

criteria.explanation: Checks for a complexity/quality gate (a configured complexity limit or a coverage threshold). Mechanical gates keep cognitive load and risk from drifting upward as the code grows.
criteria.rationale: a complexity or quality gate is configured
criteria.remediation: Configure a gate — e.g. a max-complexity rule in your linter or a coverage threshold in CI — and enforce it on PRs.

criteria.explanation: Checks for a `CLAUDE.md` project block. It is the agent's baseline briefing — build/test commands, conventions, repo layout — read at the start of every session.
criteria.rationale: a CLAUDE.md project block is present
criteria.remediation: Add a `CLAUDE.md` at the repo root, or run `/onboard-project` to scaffold the Praxion baseline blocks.

criteria.explanation: Checks for an `AGENTS.md` surface (informational — its absence does not lower the score). It provides assistant-agnostic agent instructions for non-Claude tooling.
criteria.rationale: an AGENTS.md surface is present (info, not failure)
criteria.remediation: Optionally add an `AGENTS.md` (often generated from CLAUDE.md) for assistant-agnostic agent guidance.

criteria.explanation: Checks for installed project git hooks. Hooks enforce gates (finalize, isolation checks, commit policy) automatically at the git boundary rather than relying on memory.
criteria.remediation: Install the project's git hooks — for Praxion-managed repos, run `/onboard-project` Phase 4 to symlink them.

criteria.explanation: Checks for an `.ai-state/` directory. It is the project's persistent intelligence — ADRs, decisions, metrics, tech-debt — that accrues value across agent sessions.
criteria.remediation: Create `.ai-state/` (and commit it) — `/onboard-project` scaffolds the skeleton, or add `decisions/` and a first ADR to seed it.

manageability.explanation: Praxion-native agent-manageability surfaces — CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, git hooks, and .ai-state/. Reported as a separate sub-score and never folded into the 8-pillar Factory level.

pillars.explanation: Mechanical style and validation tooling — linter, formatter, editorconfig, pre-commit, and consistent naming. Measures whether the project enforces consistency automatically so agent edits match house style without guesswork.
pillars.name: Style & Validation

pillars.explanation: How the project declares, pins, and builds its dependencies — manifest, lockfile, and CI build. Measures whether an agent can reproducibly install and build the code.
pillars.name: Build System

pillars.explanation: The automated safety net — tests on disk, run by CI, and of meaningful behavioral quality. Measures whether an agent can change code and trust a green suite to mean correct.
pillars.name: Testing

pillars.explanation: Human- and agent-facing docs — README, contributing guide, and agent-structured guidance. Measures whether the project explains itself well enough to act on.
pillars.name: Documentation

pillars.explanation: Reproducible local setup — gitignore, env-var examples, and containerization. Measures whether a contributor or agent can stand up the project the same way every time.
pillars.name: Dev Environment

pillars.explanation: Runtime visibility — logging/observability configuration and health surfaces. Measures whether an agent has evidence to diagnose failures instead of reasoning blind.
pillars.name: Debugging & Observability

pillars.explanation: Security and governance baselines — license, secrets hygiene, and dependency scanning. Measures whether the project guards against the failure modes agents are most prone to.
pillars.name: Security & Governance

pillars.explanation: Mechanical quality gates beyond style — static typing and complexity/coverage thresholds. Measures whether risk and cognitive load are held in check as the code grows.
pillars.name: Code Quality
